name: Battle of Sedan (1870)
info: Prussian and allied German armies under Moltke surrounded the French Army of Châlons at Sedan in the Franco-Prussian War, forced its surrender with Napoleon III on 2 September 1870, and the Second Empire fell two days later.

facts.date: 1 to 2 September 1870; the fighting was on 1 September and the surrender was signed at 11:30 on 2 September
facts.place: Sedan and the villages and woods around it (Bazeilles, La Moncelle, Floing, the Calvaire d'Illy and the Bois de la Garenne) on the Meuse in north-eastern France
facts.sides: France: the Army of Châlons under Marshal MacMahon, then Ducrot, then Wimpffen, with Napoleon III present, 130,000 strong, in 202 infantry battalions, 80 cavalry squadrons and 564 guns. The Prussian Third and Fourth Armies under Moltke, with King Wilhelm I and Bismarck present: 222 infantry battalions, 186 cavalry squadrons and 774 guns.
facts.outcome: The French army was surrounded and capitulated, with 104,000 men taken prisoner and 558 guns lost, and Napoleon III was taken prisoner. The war went on under a new French government.

t: The Army of Châlons was caught between the Prussian Third and Fourth Armies, driven into the Bois de la Garenne and the town by artillery fire, and surrendered on 2 September with 104,000 men and 558 guns.
The French command changed three times in a day: MacMahon was wounded, Ducrot ordered a retreat, and Wimpffen, who held a government commission to succeed MacMahon, overruled him and attacked.

Napoleon III's capture left the Prussians without an opposing government willing to make a quick peace. A Government of National Defence proclaimed on 4 September carried the war on for five more months.
dyk: Germans marked 2 September as Sedantag, the Day of Sedan, until 1919. The Kaiser himself refused to declare it an official holiday, so it stayed an unofficial day of celebration.
ev: After a hard-fought French defeat at Gravelotte on 18 August, Bazaine's Army of the Rhine retreats to Metz and is besieged there from 19 August
On 23 August the new Army of Châlons begins a left-flanking march north-east towards the Belgian border to relieve Metz
On 30 August the Prussian Fourth Army defeats MacMahon at Beaumont, and he withdraws towards Sedan
On 31 August the French deploy around Sedan while Moltke arranges his armies to encircle them
On 1 September the Germans attack from several sides, take Bazeilles, drive the French into the Bois de la Garenne and defeat the breakout attempts
On 2 September Wimpffen signs the surrender of the Army of Châlons and the fortress of Sedan
On 4 September the Second Empire collapses in a bloodless revolution and a Government of National Defence is proclaimed
On 19 September the Prussian Third and Fourth Armies begin the siege of Paris

sections.background:
After a pyrrhic victory at Gravelotte on 18 August 1870, Marshal Bazaine's Army of the Rhine, 150,000 strong, retreated to Metz, where 168,000 Prussian troops of the First and Second Armies besieged it from 19 August. Napoleon III and Marshal MacMahon formed the new Army of Châlons on 17 August to march to its rescue. From 23 August, with the emperor personally leading the army and MacMahon in attendance, it marched in a left-flanking movement north-east towards the Belgian border, meaning to avoid the Prussians before striking south to link up with Bazaine.

The Prussians had repeatedly outmanoeuvred the French through August, and the march depleted the French forces and left both flanks exposed. Leaving the First and Second Armies at Metz, Moltke took the Prussian Third and Fourth Armies northward and caught the French at the Battle of Beaumont on 30 August. MacMahon lost 7,500 men and 40 cannons there. He abandoned the planned link-up and ordered the army to withdraw north-west towards Sedan, an obsolete 17th-century fortress.

His intention was to rest an army worn by a long series of marches, resupply it with ammunition and, in his words, manoeuvre in front of the enemy. He underestimated the German strength and believed the hills around Sedan would give a major defensive advantage.
sections.forces:
The Army of Châlons was 130,000 strong. At the opening of the battle it had 202 infantry battalions, 80 cavalry squadrons and 564 guns. It faced the surrounding Prussian Third and Fourth Armies, which together had 222 infantry battalions, 186 cavalry squadrons and 774 guns. The Fourth Army, under Generalfeldmarschall Helmuth von Moltke, was accompanied by King Wilhelm I of Prussia and Chancellor Otto von Bismarck.

On arriving near Sedan on 31 August MacMahon posted Douay's 7th Corps to the north-west on the crest between the Calvaire and Floing. Ducrot's 1st Corps faced east, and Lebrun's 12th Corps garrisoned Bazeilles. General Wimpffen, newly arrived, took over 5th Corps from Failly, whose unit had been routed at Beaumont, and it was placed in reserve in the centre. The fortress covered the French rear, and the Calvaire d'Illy offered hills and woods for defence. MacMahon refused Douay's request to dig trenches, saying the army would not stay long at Sedan.

Moltke divided his forces into three groups: one to hold the French where they were, another to race forward and catch them if they retreated, and a smaller one to hold the river bank. The Saxon XII Corps crossed the Meuse, with the Prussian Guards on its right. The I Royal Bavarian Corps under von der Tann moved on Bazeilles, with two pontoon bridges laid across the Meuse by Bavarian engineers. The Prussian V and XI Corps completed the encirclement to the north-west by 09:00 on 1 September.
sections.course:
The fighting opened at Bazeilles. The French 1st Corps had barricaded the streets and enlisted the help of the townspeople. Von der Tann sent a brigade over the pontoon bridges at 04:00 in the early mist, and the Bavarians took the village by surprise. French Marines fought back from stone houses until Bavarian artillery shelled the buildings into rubble, and French brigades of the 1st, 5th and 12th Corps arrived. Bazeilles was taken at 08:00, and the artillery reached it at 09:00.

Fighting spread to La Moncelle, the one point where a breakout seemed possible. MacMahon was wounded and named Ducrot to command, who learned of it at 07:00 and ordered a retreat. Wimpffen, who held a government commission to succeed MacMahon if he were disabled, overruled him almost at once and attacked the Saxons at La Moncelle. This brought a brief French rally, which collapsed as fresh Prussian troops arrived. By 11:00 Prussian artillery had taken a toll, and a French cavalry charge was defeated by infantry and artillery fire.

German fire drove the Army of Châlons north into the Bois de la Garenne, where it was surrounded. Wimpffen ordered a breakout to the south at 13:00, but it failed. Margueritte's cavalry made three charges at Floing; he was mortally wounded in the first, and the French lost 791 killed and wounded by 15:00. The 7th Corps broke and Ducrot's 1st Corps was routed. The Prussian Guards took the Bois de la Garenne at 14:30, and the French inside surrendered. Napoleon III then hoisted a white flag on the walls of Sedan, which Wimpffen first refused to accept, launching one more attack that the Germans defeated.
sections.aftermath:
Moltke saw the white flag and sent Bronsart von Schellendorf to learn what it meant. Napoleon III sent General Reille back with a letter of surrender for the Prussian headquarters on the hillside above Frénois, and Wilhelm and Bismarck read it and Bismarck accepted it. Wimpffen asked for an honourable capitulation and for prisoner-of-war status for the army. Moltke refused, pointing to the French lack of ammunition and food, to 250,000 German troops against the 80,000 fighting for the French, and to the German position all round. The truce was extended until 09:00 on 2 September, and at 11:30 that day Wimpffen signed the surrender of the army and the fortress.

The Germans lost 9,860 men: 1,310 killed, 6,443 wounded and 2,107 missing. The Army of Châlons lost 3,220 killed and 14,811 wounded, with 104,000 taken prisoner and 558 guns, and the Germans also took 1,000 wagons and 6,000 horses. The French soldiers marched in heavy rain to an improvised prisoner-of-war camp, where they starved for the next week. On 3 September Napoleon III left for a comfortable captivity at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel.

Two days after the news reached Paris, a group of protesters stormed the imperial palace and the Second Empire collapsed in a bloodless revolution. The Government of National Defence that replaced it carried on the war for five more months before becoming the Third Republic. The Prussian Third and Fourth Armies besieged Paris from 19 September.
sections.sources:
MacMahon's stated intention at Sedan was to rest and resupply the army and, in his words, manoeuvre in front of the enemy. When Wimpffen sought an honourable capitulation, Moltke answered with the French lack of ammunition and food and with a count of 250,000 German troops against 80,000 fighting for the French. That count stands beside the 130,000 given for the Army of Châlons as a whole.

The French command passed from MacMahon to Ducrot to Wimpffen in the course of the morning.
sections.legacy:
The defeat at Sedan, the capture of Napoleon III and of France's second army, with the first French army shut up in Metz, is held to have sealed the outcome of the war in Prussia's favour. The new French government fought on, so the surrender ended the Empire and not the war. The Government of National Defence proclaimed on 4 September carried the war on for five more months before becoming the Third Republic.

In recognition of the part the battle played in German unification, many Germans celebrated Sedantag, the Day of Sedan, on each 2 September until 1919. The Kaiser himself refused to declare it an official holiday, and it remained an unofficial day of celebration. Napoleon III spent his captivity at Schloss Wilhelmshöhe near Kassel, and the French prisoners watched him leave on 3 September with disinterest.

summary: On 1 and 2 September 1870 the Prussian Third and Fourth Armies surrounded the French Army of Châlons at Sedan, and 104,000 French soldiers and Napoleon III were taken. The Second Empire fell on 4 September, but the war went on under a new government.
references: M. Howard, The Franco-Prussian War: The German Invasion of France 1870–1871 (Rupert Hart-Davis, 1961)
Terence Zuber, The Moltke Myth: Prussian War Planning, 1857–1871 (University Press of America, 2008)
notes: The article's lead says the battle 'effectively decided the war in favour of Prussia' and calls it 'a battle of annihilation'; I kept the first (attributed as 'is held') and left out the second.

Figures that stand beside each other: 130,000 for the Army of Châlons (lead) against the 80,000 'fighting for the French' that Moltke cites; the French battalion/gun totals are given in the article and I kept them. The article gives the French as 104,000 captured, killed 3,220 and wounded 14,811 which together exceed the 130,000 less the 80,000; I add nothing up.

The sources section is thin because the article names no chronicler or historian, only the participants. Its second paragraph is my reading of the article's own conflicting times; the editor may cut it.

Time inconsistencies in the article: fighting 'began in earnest at 06:00' while Ducrot learned of his command at 07:00; the 8th Infantry Division arrives at 08:00 yet the Prussian V and XI Corps are in position at 07:30 and 09:00. Bazeilles is said to be taken in the morning rush and again 'taken at 08:00'. I used the times without reconciling them.
The article calls Gravelotte a 'pyrrhic victory' (no whose); the 150,000 Army of the Rhine is Bazaine's. The ev entry 1870 for Gravelotte is dated by the article as 18 August.

Left out: the two epigraph quotations ('mousetrap', 'chamber pot'), the Empress's remark, Margueritte's first name details, pontoon detail, Douay's trenches above Floing, and the article's 'Prussian' vs 'German' mixture: I used the article's names for each corps. Mentions of Wimpffen's 'commission from the government' kept as the article gives it.
The Bois de la Garenne sentence says French inside 'surrendered' at 14:30; Napoleon's white flag follows it. The 791 figure is French killed and wounded in the cavalry charges at Floing.
